title: Advances in LLMs with Focus on Reasoning, Adaptability, Efficiency, and Ethics

bias_targets.methodology: Surveyed through literature review of case studies, including historical hiring algorithms favoring men, higher error rates for female faces in commercial facial recognition models (e.g., the 'Gender Shades' study), and medical AI models missing diseases in women. The paper discusses evaluating these biases using fairness tools (e.g., AI Fairness 360) and metrics like demographic parity and equalized odds.

Reviewed via existing literature documenting disparate impacts, such as unjust legal and sentencing rulings against minority communities, healthcare AI trained primarily on white male patients missing diseases in people of color, and higher error rates for darker skin tones in facial recognition. The paper highlights quantifying these inequities using metrics like disparate impact and equalized odds.

Discussed in the context of financial applications, specifically AI-driven credit scoring and loan approval systems that may unfairly reject low-income individuals based on biased historical data. Evaluation relies on algorithmic fairness audits and explainability tools mandated by risk management frameworks.
